transcript.text: Hi, our integrated fridge freezer (behind a kitchen door) - the fridge is around 10 degrees but the freezer seems ok. We had a power cut a week ago, not sure if related. Rented flat, can't really take it out.

A fridge at ~10°C is too warm for safe food storage. It should be about 3–5°C (and ideally below 5°C). The freezer should be -18°C.

Because it is rented and integrated, don’t try to pull it out or dismantle it. Do this:

1. Check the temperature with a separate fridge thermometer if possible, placed in a glass of water in the middle of the fridge for a few hours. Built-in displays can be inaccurate.
2. Check settings: make sure it has not been put into holiday/demo/eco mode after the power cut. Set the fridge colder (e.g. 3–4°C) and allow several hours.
3. Check the door seals and kitchen cupboard door: an integrated appliance can be held slightly open if the cabinet door hinges/sliders are misaligned or something is stopping it closing. Look for gaps, warm air, condensation, or the internal light staying on.
4. Don’t block internal air vents with food, and check for heavy ice/frost on the back wall or around vents. A blocked fan/air channel can leave the fridge warm while the freezer still seems fine.
5. Report it to the landlord/agent now as an urgent appliance repair, including the temperature, the recent power cut, and that the freezer appears normal. Take a photo of the thermometer/display and note times/settings. They should arrange an engineer; an integrated fridge-freezer may need a fan, thermostat/sensor, damper, or defrost-system repair.

Food safety: if food has genuinely been sitting around 10°C for more than a few hours, be cautious. Discard high-risk chilled foods such as cooked meat, fish, ready meals, dairy, soft cheese, opened chilled foods, and leftovers if you cannot be confident they have stayed below about 8°C. Don’t rely on smell alone. Keep the door shut as much as possible and consider a cool box/another fridge for essentials.

Avoid switching it off or repeatedly power-cycling it unless the landlord/engineer advises, as that could thaw the freezer. If it is hot at the sides/back beyond normal, making burning smells, sparking, or tripping electrics, unplug it and report it immediately.

Thanks. There's no display, just a dial inside, and it's on 3 out of 5. I put a separate thermometer in the fridge and it also says about 10C, and the freezer one says about -16C. The fridge door closes fine and the cabinet door moves with it. There's a bit of frost on the freezer back wall, not loads, and I can't see any vents in the fridge. No burning smell or tripping. Should I turn the dial up?

Yes — on most fridge-freezers, a higher number means colder. Turn it from 3 to 4, or even 5 temporarily if 4 makes no difference, then leave it alone with the door shut as much as possible.

A few points:

• Give it at least 12 hours, ideally 24 hours, before judging the result. Avoid changing the dial repeatedly.
• Put the thermometer in a glass of water in the middle of the fridge, not touching the back wall, for a more reliable reading.
• Aim for 3–5°C in the fridge. The freezer at -16°C is not disastrous but is also slightly warmer than the usual target of -18°C, which supports the possibility that the appliance is not cooling properly overall.
• A small amount of frost on the freezer back wall can be normal. Thick frost/ice would be more concerning.

However, I would still report this to the landlord/agent today, rather than waiting for it to fail completely. Say something like:

> “Integrated fridge-freezer fridge compartment is holding at around 10°C on an independent thermometer; freezer is around -16°C. This began/was noticed after last week’s power cut. I have checked the doors close properly and have turned the thermostat up. Please arrange repair urgently.”

If it remains above 5–8°C after 24 hours on the colder setting, treat it as faulty and avoid keeping perishable food in it.
